ruling_text:
As to Objections: The Court would OVERRULE Defendants National and Integron’s evidentiary
objections. As to Plaintiffs’ objections to the Opposition’s reference to pictures without
support, the Court would also OVERULE. Objections lie to evidence, not in argument.
As to Class Certification: The Court would GRANT the motion and CERTIFY a class and sub-class
(defined below) under their 1st and 3rd causes of action for all purposes (but solely related to
recovering collision and punitive damages). The Court would ORDER the following:
(a) The Class is defined as: “All individuals who satisfy the following criteria: (1) the
individual was a named insured on a California automobile insurance policy that was
underwritten by Integon National Insurance Company; (2) the individual or another
named insured on that individual’s policy was involved in an automobile accident
while driving an insured vehicle; (3) a post-accident claim was made under the policy
for losses from that accident; (4) the individual had his or her insurance policy
rescinded between May 14, 2015, and the present (“Class Period”); (5) the individual
had his or her insurance policy rescinded after a claim was made under the policy;
(6) the individual had his or her insurance policy rescinded for failure to disclose
household members on the insurance application; and (7) the individual suffered
losses because of the policy rescission;”
(b) The Renewal Sub-Class is defined as “All Class Members whose automobile
insurance policies renewed during the Class Period;”
(c) Plaintiffs Emily Cobos, Christian Angel, Yuriana Aparacio, Tiana Vale, Robert
Gallegos, Luis Sanchez, Jessica Chang, Crystal Flowers, Andy Nguyen, Charles Smith,
Javier Hurtado, Carlos Andrade, Arlene Martinez, Sally Greene, and Danielle Tolkson
are the Class Representatives of the Class;
(d) Plaintiff Emily Cobos is Class Representative of the Renewal Sub-Class;
(e) Attorneys Jonathan King and Justin King of the Law Offices of Justin King are Class
Counsel;

Class Counsel are ORDERED to prepare and submit an order on the certification of the class and
sub-class that complies with Rule 3.765 of the Rules of Court within 5 court days.
Parties are also ORDERED to meet and confer on providing class notice of the certification
within the next 15 days and submit a joint proposed class notice and procedure within 30 days
per Rules of Court, rule 3.766.

Case Summary
This is essentially an insurance bad faith class action. Proposed class members are named
insureds on automobile policies with Defendants. Plaintiffs allege that when post-accident
claims were made, Defendants retroactively rescinded the policies on the grounds that
household members, who were fourteen or older, were not disclosed on the initial insurance
application. The rescission took place despite the fact that the undisclosed household member
was not the driver at the time of the relevant accident. Plaintiffs allege that the application
system forced applicants to represent that all disclosures of household members had been
made, despite preventing that very disclosure.

On May 14, 2019, Plaintiffs Emily Cobos, Christian Angel, Stephanie Camacho, Yuriana Aparacio,
and Griselda Davila, on behalf of themselves and all others similarly situated, filed the original
class action against defendants National General Insurance Company (National) and Integon
National Insurance Company (Integon). Since that date, this matter has been through four
amendments: A First Amended Complaint (FAC) was filed on June 6, 2019, which added Tiana
Vale as an additional plaintiff. On October 16, 2019, following Defendants’ Demurrer, Plaintiffs
filed a Second Amended Complaint. On October 1, 2020, after the Court granted leave to
amend, Plaintiffs filed a Third Amended Complaint (TAC). The TAC added plaintiffs Jessica
Chang, Crystal Flowers, Andy Nguyen, Charles Smith, Javier Hurtado, Marco Avilla, Carlos
Andrade, Arlene Martinez, Sally Greene, Danielle Tolkson, and Taina Vale. Plaintiffs also added
defendants National General Insurance Group (National Group), Stonewood Insurance Services,
Inc., All Star General Insurance Agency, Inc., All Star General Insurance Company, New
Millennium Insurance, Freeway Insurance Services, Inc., One Way Insurance Services, Jack
Olivera Insurance Services, Cost-U-Less Insurance Center, Marisol’s Insurance Services, Inc.,
Auto Club Services, LLC, Torres & Associates, First Contempo Insurance Agency, Fiesta Auto
Insurance Center, and Upgrade Insurance Services, Inc. On February 11, 2021, Plaintiffs named
Doe 1 to the TAC, adding National General Management Corp. Between March 19, 2021 and
August 11, 2022, Plaintiffs dismissed all defendants except National, Integron, National Group,
National General Management Corporation, and All Star General Insurance Company. Finally,
on December 15, 2022, Plaintiffs were granted leave to file their Fourth Amended Complaint
(4th AC). With the 4th AC, Plaintiffs (1) revised the class definition and allegations to cover all
damages, not just automobile collision damages, from Defendants’ rescission of automobile
insurance policies; (2) removed 4 of the 19 putative class representatives; and (3) removed the
Defendants dismissed from the action and deleted allegations related to those Defendants. The
only Defendants named in the proposed 4th AC are now National, Integron, and National
Group. Notably, the 4th AC has 79 causes of class and individual causes of action.
Summary of the Law
A trial court has great discretion in certifying class actions. (Bell v. American Title Ins. Co. (1991)
226 Cal.App.3d 1589, 1606.) In a motion for class certification, plaintiffs must demonstrate
through substantial evidence that the proposed class is ascertainable; that its members are
numerous; that the plaintiffs’ claims are typical of claims held by other class members; that
plaintiffs and counsel can provide adequate representation for the class; and that common
questions of law or fact predominate over the individual issues. (Brinker Restaurant Corp. v.
Superior Court (2012) 53 Cal.4th 1004, 1021-1022.) Certifying a class action requires a
demonstrated substantial benefit to litigants and court. (Caro v. Proctor & Gamble Co. (1993) 18
Cal.App.4th 644, 657.) The burden of this demonstration rests with plaintiff. (Collins v. Safeway
Stores, Inc. (1986) 187 Cal.App.3d 62.)
Analysis
The Court previously found the proposed class was sufficiently numerous and ascertainable, the
Class Representative Plaintiffs were typical with the putative class and adequate, Plaintiffs’
Counsel was adequate class counsel, and common questions on liability issues predominate.
Under the Court of Appeal’s decision, the class as proposed by movants – at minimum on
Defendants’ liability – shall be certified. Thus, the Court need not re-analyze these points.
Therefore, the sole issues herein are two-fold: fold (1) certifying a sub-class for solely class
members whose policies were renewed and (2) whether the certified class will include the issue
of damages, as limited to collision coverage damages (lesser of the vehicle’s repair cost and its
fair market value) and punitive damages.

As to a Sub-Class: Defendants do not oppose a sub-class for class members whose policies were
renewed. In the Reply filed on September 29, 2022, Plaintiffs raised a sub-class headed by
Plaintiff Cobos, as she had renewed her policy. The Court would propose the sub-class as “All
Class Members whose automobile insurance policies renewed during the Class Period.”
As to Damages: The sought damages in the class certified-liability claims are collision damages
and punitive damages. It seems undisputed that no individual inquiry would be necessary
related to the recovery of punitive damages whether adjudicated within the liability phase or
bifurcated for separate adjudication. The dispute lies over whether the collision damages
should be adjudicated on class-wide basis or not. Therein lies the initial concern of whether
common questions will predominate or can be managed.
Even if the damages of each putative class member may require some individual showing such
does not preclude class certification as long as they can be managed. (Sav-on Drug Stores, Inc.
v. Superior Court (2004) 34 Cal.4th 319, 332, 334.) Damages can be proven by the use of
statistical evidence, sampling evidence, or expert testimony as such “does not dispense with
proof of damages but rather offers a different method of proof.” (Id. at p. 333.) Furthermore,
when fact of damages is certain, the amount of damages need not be calculated with
mathematical certainty. (Michelson v. Hamada (1994) 29 Cal.App.4th 1566, 1585.)
Here, Class Plaintiffs present their trial plan and an expert report where their expert reviewed
180 sampling claim files. Of the 180 claim files, 177 or 98.3% had collision coverage.
Furthermore, 160 of the 180 claims filed contained estimates for collision coverage that those
insured would have been entitled to recover. On these numbers, under an extrapolation, 84-
92% of the 1,032 currently known class members (or 866-954) should have collision damages
information in their claim file to establish their collision damages. Of the 78-166 claim files that
may not have this information, Plaintiffs’ counsel indicates an estimate may be done based on
estimated damage repairs. (King Decl., ¶5 & Exh. 1 [¶¶10, 21, 23-24].)
For purposes of certification, the above demonstrates that – for a majority of the class
members – their claim file appears likely to provide the information to determine damages. For
a minority of the class members, however, their claim file will lack that information.
Nonetheless, it appears that statistical averaging and estimating can be used to support
providing an aggregate damage amount for any judgment. This mitigates the likelihood of
manageability concerns on this aspect of damages.

Moreover, for the purposes of certification, the law is unconcerned as to how any aggregate
judgment is allocated. (Bell v. Farmers Ins. Exchange (2004) 115 Cal.App.4th 715, 759 [“It is well
established that ‘the allocation of that aggregate sum [of the judgment] among class members
is an internal class accounting question that does not directly concern the defendant . . . .’
[Citation.]”].) That allocation is done as a separate proceeding. (In re Cipro Cases I & II (2004)
121 Cal.App.4th 402, 417 [“If the defendant in a class action is found liable, and there is a
finding at trial as to the amount of class-wide damages, each class member’s individual
entitlement to damages may be litigated in a nonadversary administrative claims procedure
with a lowered standard of proof.”].)
While the Court still has some apprehension about manageability, if for some reason the issue
of the collision damages recoverable by class members whose claim files lack any repair data
become unmanageable, the Court could consider decertifying their damage portion and hold
individual separate trials on those putative class members’ damages. Any certification order is
only tentative as it may be modified any time before the trial. (Vasquez v. Superior Court (1971)
4 Cal.3d 800, 821; Estrada v. RPS, Inc. (2005) 125 Cal.App.4th 976, 980-981.)
